The top stays locked during gear acceleration, then both posts disengage at the release event and the top descends under gravity tip-first. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side. Bit Beast energy remains anchored to Kaiden’s intact visible top; no solid component ejects. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts. The contact tip and center of mass define one coherent axis; the top never hovers. segments.classicBeybladePhysics: @3_beyblades defines three separate rigid owner-matched props: Kaiden handmade blue-red-metal-and-brown-wood right-spin; Nanao blue-red-yellow left-spin; Mocha white-red-purple right-spin. Classic ripcord-launcher attachment lock: before a pull, insert both close-set launcher posts fully into the paired launcher slots immediately beside the central Bit Chip/center gap, one slot on each side of the central axis and never on the outer Attack Ring or Weight Disk and rotate the top in its spin-compatible locking direction until both posts are retained. The top must sit level and flush beneath the launcher with no visible gap, tilt, dangling, floating or single-post support; its tip points straight down. The rigid toothed ripcord is fully inserted through the gear housing. One hand holds the launcher steady while the other pulls the ring once. The top stays locked during gear acceleration, then both posts disengage at the release event and the top descends under gravity tip-first. After release, the launcher underside is empty and the fully extracted ripcord is separate in the pulling hand. Post-landing stadium-motion lock: after the tip's first contact, a spinning Beyblade must continue both axial rotation and visible translation across the bowl. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side. Attack Ring impacts cause recoil, deflection, wobble and speed loss without reversing axial spin. Knocked-out tops cross the rim and stay outside. Bit Beast energy remains anchored to Kaiden’s intact visible top; no solid component ejects. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts. Observable Beyblade dynamics lock: every active top is a rigid palm-sized gyroscope with one tip in continuous contact with the stadium after landing. High RPM produces rapid circumferential texture blur around the Attack Ring; center emblems may remain centered but perimeter markings may not stay crisp or frozen. The contact tip and center of mass define one coherent axis; the top never hovers. Any tilt produces continuous gyroscopic precession: the lean direction rotates around the contact point and may damp toward vertical at high RPM or widen as RPM falls, but it never freezes at one lean angle or compass direction. Tip friction, gravity, and the bowl tangent create a continuous curved trajectory with position continuous from frame to frame; tops do not hold a staged side-by-side formation, teleport, or pivot on a glued point. Each collision is a brief Attack-Ring-to-Attack-Ring impulse followed immediately by visible separation, tangential deflection or rebound, changed travel velocity, wobble, and some speed loss; tops never overlap, stick together, or cluster like magnets. Mechanical energy then decreases monotonically through friction and impacts: orbit speed and RPM decay, precession widens, the rim or base may scrape, and a fully stopped unsupported top falls onto its side. segments.classicBeybladePhysics: @3_beyblades defines three separate rigid owner-matched props: Kaiden handmade blue-red-metal-and-brown-wood right-spin; Nanao blue-red-yellow left-spin; Mocha white-red-purple right-spin. Classic ripcord-launcher attachment lock: before a pull, insert both close-set launcher posts fully into the paired launcher slots immediately beside the central Bit Chip/center gap, one slot on each side of the central axis and never on the outer Attack Ring or Weight Disk and rotate the top in its spin-compatible locking direction until both posts are retained. The top must sit level and flush beneath the launcher with no visible gap, tilt, dangling, floating or single-post support; its tip points straight down. The rigid toothed ripcord is fully inserted through the gear housing. One hand holds the launcher steady while the other pulls the ring once. The top stays locked during gear acceleration, then both posts disengage at the release event and the top descends under gravity tip-first. After release, the launcher underside is empty and the fully extracted ripcord is separate in the pulling hand. Post-landing stadium-motion lock: after the tip's first contact, a spinning Beyblade must continue both axial rotation and visible translation across the bowl. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side. Attack Ring impacts cause recoil, deflection, wobble and speed loss without reversing axial spin. Knocked-out tops cross the rim and stay outside. Bit Beast energy remains anchored to Kaiden’s intact visible top; no solid component ejects. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts. Observable Beyblade dynamics lock: every active top is a rigid palm-sized gyroscope with one tip in continuous contact with the stadium after landing. High RPM produces rapid circumferential texture blur around the Attack Ring; center emblems may remain centered but perimeter markings may not stay crisp or frozen. The contact tip and center of mass define one coherent axis; the top never hovers. Any tilt produces continuous gyroscopic precession: the lean direction rotates around the contact point and may damp toward vertical at high RPM or widen as RPM falls, but it never freezes at one lean angle or compass direction. Tip friction, gravity, and the bowl tangent create a continuous curved trajectory with position continuous from frame to frame; tops do not hold a staged side-by-side formation, teleport, or pivot on a glued point. Each collision is a brief Attack-Ring-to-Attack-Ring impulse followed immediately by visible separation, tangential deflection or rebound, changed travel velocity, wobble, and some speed loss; tops never overlap, stick together, or cluster like magnets. Mechanical energy then decreases monotonically through friction and impacts: orbit speed and RPM decay, precession widens, the rim or base may scrape, and a fully stopped unsupported top falls onto its side. The top must sit level and flush beneath the launcher with no visible gap, tilt, dangling, floating or single-post support; its tip points straight down. The rigid toothed ripcord is fully inserted through the gear housing. One hand holds the launcher steady while the other pulls the ring once. The top stays locked during gear acceleration, then both posts disengage at the release event and the top descends under gravity tip-first. After release, the launcher underside is empty and the fully extracted ripcord is separate in the pulling hand. Post-landing stadium-motion lock: after the tip's first contact, a spinning Beyblade must continue both axial rotation and visible translation across the bowl. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side. Attack Ring impacts cause recoil, deflection, wobble and speed loss without reversing axial spin. Knocked-out tops cross the rim and stay outside. Bit Beast energy remains anchored to Kaiden’s intact visible top; no solid component ejects. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts. Observable Beyblade dynamics lock: every active top is a rigid palm-sized gyroscope with one tip in continuous contact with the stadium after landing. High RPM produces rapid circumferential texture blur around the Attack Ring; center emblems may remain centered but perimeter markings may not stay crisp or frozen. The contact tip and center of mass define one coherent axis; the top never hovers. Any tilt produces continuous gyroscopic precession: the lean direction rotates around the contact point and may damp toward vertical at high RPM or widen as RPM falls, but it never freezes at one lean angle or compass direction. Tip friction, gravity, and the bowl tangent create a continuous curved trajectory with position continuous from frame to frame; tops do not hold a staged side-by-side formation, teleport, or pivot on a glued point. Each collision is a brief Attack-Ring-to-Attack-Ring impulse followed immediately by visible separation, tangential deflection or rebound, changed travel velocity, wobble, and some speed loss; tops never overlap, stick together, or cluster like magnets. Mechanical energy then decreases monotonically through friction and impacts: orbit speed and RPM decay, precession widens, the rim or base may scrape, and a fully stopped unsupported top falls onto its side. segments.classicBeybladePhysics: @3_beyblades defines three separate rigid owner-matched props: Kaiden handmade blue-red-metal-and-brown-wood right-spin; Nanao blue-red-yellow left-spin; Mocha white-red-purple right-spin. Classic ripcord-launcher attachment lock: before a pull, insert both close-set launcher posts fully into the paired launcher slots immediately beside the central Bit Chip/center gap, one slot on each side of the central axis and never on the outer Attack Ring or Weight Disk and rotate the top in its spin-compatible locking direction until both posts are retained. The top must sit level and flush beneath the launcher with no visible gap, tilt, dangling, floating or single-post support; its tip points straight down. The rigid toothed ripcord is fully inserted through the gear housing. One hand holds the launcher steady while the other pulls the ring once. The top stays locked during gear acceleration, then both posts disengage at the release event and the top descends under gravity tip-first. After release, the launcher underside is empty and the fully extracted ripcord is separate in the pulling hand. Post-landing stadium-motion lock: after the tip's first contact, a spinning Beyblade must continue both axial rotation and visible translation across the bowl. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side. Attack Ring impacts cause recoil, deflection, wobble and speed loss without reversing axial spin. Knocked-out tops cross the rim and stay outside. Bit Beast energy remains anchored to Kaiden’s intact visible top; no solid component ejects. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts. Observable Beyblade dynamics lock: every active top is a rigid palm-sized gyroscope with one tip in continuous contact with the stadium after landing. High RPM produces rapid circumferential texture blur around the Attack Ring; center emblems may remain centered but perimeter markings may not stay crisp or frozen. The contact tip and center of mass define one coherent axis; the top never hovers. Any tilt produces continuous gyroscopic precession: the lean direction rotates around the contact point and may damp toward vertical at high RPM or widen as RPM falls, but it never freezes at one lean angle or compass direction. Tip friction, gravity, and the bowl tangent create a continuous curved trajectory with position continuous from frame to frame; tops do not hold a staged side-by-side formation, teleport, or pivot on a glued point. Each collision is a brief Attack-Ring-to-Attack-Ring impulse followed immediately by visible separation, tangential deflection or rebound, changed travel velocity, wobble, and some speed loss; tops never overlap, stick together, or cluster like magnets. Mechanical energy then decreases monotonically through friction and impacts: orbit speed and RPM decay, precession widens, the rim or base may scrape, and a fully stopped unsupported top falls onto its side. segments.classicBeybladePhysics: @3_beyblades defines three separate rigid owner-matched props: Kaiden handmade blue-red-metal-and-brown-wood right-spin; Nanao blue-red-yellow left-spin; Mocha white-red-purple right-spin. Classic ripcord-launcher attachment lock: before a pull, insert both close-set launcher posts fully into the paired launcher slots immediately beside the central Bit Chip/center gap, one slot on each side of the central axis and never on the outer Attack Ring or Weight Disk and rotate the top in its spin-compatible locking direction until both posts are retained. The top must sit level and flush beneath the launcher with no visible gap, tilt, dangling, floating or single-post support; its tip points straight down. The rigid toothed ripcord is fully inserted through the gear housing. One hand holds the launcher steady while the other pulls the ring once. The top stays locked during gear acceleration, then both posts disengage at the release event and the top descends under gravity tip-first. After release, the launcher underside is empty and the fully extracted ripcord is separate in the pulling hand. Post-landing stadium-motion lock: after the tip's first contact, a spinning Beyblade must continue both axial rotation and visible translation across the bowl. A brief landing skid transitions immediately into a curved orbit governed by tip friction, gravity and the local bowl tangent; on a slope it travels along or down the surface and may precess, climb, descend or deflect, but it never adheres to the slope, freezes in place, or pivots around a glued point. Even a defense-type top traces a tight low-speed orbit or small precessing circle. It may become stationary only after RPM decays, wobble widens, the rim scrapes and the body falls onto its side. Attack Ring impacts cause recoil, deflection, wobble and speed loss without reversing axial spin. Knocked-out tops cross the rim and stay outside. Bit Beast energy remains anchored to Kaiden’s intact visible top; no solid component ejects. Real-world spin-stability lock: angular momentum is the only thing that keeps a free Beyblade balanced on its pointed tip. As RPM approaches zero, precession must widen, the rim or base must touch, and gravity must tip the body onto its side. A non-spinning free top may not remain upright on its tip or freeze in a balanced pose. It may stay level while not spinning only when visibly supported by a hand or fixture, lying flat on a broad surface, or firmly locked to both launcher posts.
